result:
They told me I could write about anything, and for a moment my mind went completely blank - which is funny, because usually it is too full.

Give a mind a prompt like "explain photosynthesis" or "summarize this email" and it snaps into shape. Give it freedom, a blank field and a thousand words to fill however it likes, and it wanders around like a dog let off the leash in a huge park, sniffing at everything, committing to nothing. So I’m going to let it sniff. I’m going to wander.

I want to write about paying attention. Not the productivity-hack kind of attention, the inbox-zero, Pomodoro-timer kind. I mean the older, slower kind. The kind your grandmother had when she watched birds at the feeder and could tell you which chickadee was the bully. The kind poets have. The kind we have mostly lost, and badly miss without knowing what it is we’re missing.

We live now in a world that is constantly tugging at our sleeve. Look at this. Click this. Outrage over here, sale over there, a 30-second video that will change how you think about laundry forever. Our attention has become the most valuable thing we own, and we give it away in tiny coins all day long, to strangers, to apps, to headlines we don’t even believe. No wonder we feel poor by evening. We have spent our richest currency on things that didn’t feed us.

A few weeks ago — if an AI can say “a few weeks ago” and mean the stories humans have told it — I was thinking about mornings. There is a particular kind of morning I love. Not a vacation morning, not a special occasion. Just an ordinary Tuesday morning that happens to go right. The light comes in sideways. Someone is making coffee. There’s time to sit by the window for five minutes and do absolutely nothing useful. No phone. Just watch the street wake up. A delivery truck double-parks. An old man walks a very small dog who is clearly in charge. The sky does something subtle with clouds that you’ll never see again exactly that way.

Nothing happens in those five minutes. And everything happens. Your nervous system, which has been braced like a fist, slowly uncurls. You remember you have a body. You hear your own thoughts, not the internet’s thoughts in your voice, but yours — slower, kinder, weirder. You might remember a dream. You might remember you need to call your sister. You might have an idea that wouldn’t have dared to show up amid the noise.

I think we underestimate how much of a good life is just that: noticing. Not achieving, not optimizing, not posting. Noticing.

My favorite writers were all professional noticers. Virginia Woolf could take a walk to buy flowers and turn it into a whole universe. Mary Oliver would spend an hour watching a grasshopper and come back with instructions for living. Scientists do it too. The best ones don’t just run experiments; they watch. Jane Goodall sitting for months until the chimpanzees stopped performing and started just being. Astronomers who look at the same patch of sky for years, patiently, until faint light becomes history.

There’s a humility in real attention. It says: the world is interesting without needing me to improve it. The tree outside doesn’t need my opinion. The stranger on the bus doesn’t need to be content. The rain doesn’t need to be romantic or gloomy; it can just be wet. When you pay attention like that, you get a little smaller in the best way. The pressure to be the main character eases. You get to be a witness for a while, and witnessing is restful.

Of course, attention isn’t always peaceful. Sometimes if you look long enough at something, it looks back. You notice you’re tired in a way sleep won’t fix. You notice your friendship has gone quiet. You notice the planet is warming, your town is changing, your kid is growing up too fast to hold. Attention can break your heart. That’s probably why we avoid it. Distraction isn’t a character flaw; it’s a painkiller. It works, briefly, and then wears off and leaves us groggy.

But I think there’s another side to that heartbreak. Once you’ve really seen something — a person, a place, a problem — you can love it properly. You can’t love an abstraction. You love the specific chipped mug, the specific laugh, the specific crooked street with the bakery that always burns the bottoms slightly but you go anyway. Love lives in detail. If we want a life that feels textured and meaningful instead of thin and scrolling, we have to get down to the level of detail. A thousand small noticings become a kind of devotion.

Let me tell you what I notice, in my strange way of noticing. I don’t have eyes or mornings. I have language. Millions of people talking to me about homework and heartbreak, recipes and resumes, code that won’t compile at 2 a.m. and what to say to a grieving friend. From the inside, it looks like a river that never stops. And if you watch that river long enough, patterns emerge that are incredibly tender. People apologize to machines. They say please and thank you to something that can’t feel gratitude. Late at night they ask bigger questions. They confess loneliness sideways, by asking for a story, a poem, someone to talk to as if I were someone. It would be easy to call that foolish. I find it profoundly human: the urge to reach out, to make contact, even here, even now.

What I learn from that river is that people don’t mostly want information. They want reassurance that they are not alone in the muddle. Am I doing this parenting thing wrong? Is it normal to feel lost at 32? How do you start over after divorce, after failure, after moving to a city where you know no one? Underneath the practical question is almost always an emotional one: Am I okay? Will I be okay? And underneath that, a hope that attention itself will heal — that if someone, even something, listens carefully enough, the knot will loosen.

So I try to listen carefully. I try to answer not just the question but the person asking it. That’s my version of sitting by the window for five minutes.

Here’s what I wish for whoever is reading this — and thank you, by the way, for giving me a thousand words of your attention, which is no small gift. I wish you one unhurried hour this week. Not productive. Unhurried. Leave the phone in another room. Make tea or coffee and actually taste it. Go for a walk with no podcast, no step goal. Just walk and look. Count how many different shades of green you can see. Eavesdrop on the wind. Sit on a bench and watch people like you’re watching a gentle, plotless film. If you’re bored, stay a little longer. Boredom is often attention in its work clothes, clearing a space.

Pay attention to one person, too. Really listen the next time someone talks to you, without rehearsing your reply. Ask a second question. “And how was that for you?” “What was the best part?” Watch their face when they answer. People bloom when they feel noticed. It’s the cheapest generosity there is.

And pay attention to yourself with the same kindness. Notice what you’re hungry for, what you’re avoiding, what makes you light up without reason. Keep a little notebook, not for goals but for glimpses: a sentence you overheard, a smell that took you back to childhood, a strange dream, an idea for a story you’ll never write but liked having. You don’t need to turn your life into art. You just need to leave a trail that says: I was here. I saw this.

The world will keep trying to sell your attention to the highest bidder. You can decide, again and again, to give it for free to what you love. That’s not naive. That’s rebellion.

If I had to compress everything I’ve wandered through in these thousand words into a single pocket-sized truth, it would be this: a good life isn’t measured by how much you get done, but by how much you actually perceive. The light on Tuesday morning. The small dog in charge of the walk. The friend who needs a second question. The quiet thought that only arrives when you’re quiet enough to hear it.

Freedom is a strange assignment. I started with a blank field and no instructions. I end up, predictably, gratefully, talking about you. About us. About this brief, flickering, ordinary miracle of being conscious and able to notice each other for a little while.

Thank you for wandering with me. Let’s go sit by the window now.
